title: Conventions
body_md: Throughout this paper, spanning surfaces are assumed to be compact and connected, but they are not assumed to be oriented or even orientable.
head: manual

label: defn:conc
title: Definition
head: environment
name: Turaev

label: equivalence
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{equivalence}
Two spanning surfaces are \textit{$S^*$-equivalent} if one can be obtained from the other by (i) ambient isotopy, (ii) attachment (or removal) of a tube, and (iii) attachment (or removal) of a half-twisted band.
head: environment

label: boundary
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{boundary}
Let $W$ be a compact oriented 3-manifold with $\partial W=\Sigma$. Assume that $E\subset W\times I$ is a closed nonorientable surface with $[E]=0$ in $H_2(W\times I; {\mathbb Z}/2)$ and with normal Euler number $e(E)=0$. Then there exists a compact 3-manifold $V\subset W\times I$ with $\partial V=E$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Every nonorientable surface $E$ can be written as a connected sum of ${\mathbb R}{\rm P}^2$, and in this context, a surface with $E = \#_{i=1}^{g} {\mathbb R}{\rm P}^2$ is said to have nonorientable genus $g$. A routine calculation shows that 
$$H_i(E;{\mathbb Z})= \begin{cases} {\mathbb Z} & \text{if $i=0,$}\\
{\mathbb Z}/2 \oplus {\mathbb Z}^{g-1}& \text{if $i=1,$}
                     
\end{cases}\quad \text{and} \quad
H_i(E;{\mathbb Z}/2)= \begin{cases} {\mathbb Z}/2 & \text{if $i=0,2,$}\\
({\mathbb Z}/2)^{g}& \text{if $i=1.$}
                      
\end{cases}$$

In this case, the assumption that $e(E)=0$ implies that $E$ has nonorientable genus $g=2k$. Thus $E$ abstractly bounds a 3-manifold. This fact, together with the assumption that $[E]=0$ in $H_2(W \times I;{\mathbb Z}/2),$ implies that $E$ is trivial in ${\mathfrak N}_2(W \times I)$, the unoriented bordism group, by Theorem 17.1 of \cite{Conner-Floyd}. It remains to show that $E$ bounds a 3-manifold embedded in $W \times I$.

Let $N_E$ be a tubular neighborhood of $E$ in $W\times I$ and let $S_E$ be its boundary. Then $N_E$ is a $D^2$ bundle over $E$ isomorphic to the normal bundle $\nu(E)$  to the embedding $j \colon E \to W\times I$, and $S_E$ is the associated $S^1$-bundle. Since $\nu(E)\oplus TE \cong j^*(T(W\times I))$ and $W\times I$ is orientable, it follows that $w_1(\nu(E)) = w_1(E).$

Although the normal bundle $\nu(E)$ is not orientable, it has an Euler class in $H^{2}(E;{\mathbb Z}_w),$ cohomology with coefficients twisted by the representation $w\colon \pi_1(E) \to \{\pm 1\}$ associated to the first Stiefel-Whitney class $w_1(E)$ \cite{Massey}. Poincar\'{e} duality for twisted coefficients (cf.~Theorem 5.7 in \cite{Davis-Kirk}) implies that $H^2(E; {\mathbb Z}_w) \cong H_0(E;{\mathbb Z}).$ Thus the Euler class is determined by an integer, namely the normal Euler number $e(E).$ Since $e(E)=0$, the bundle $\nu(E)$ admits a nowhere zero section, which we use to split $\nu(E) = L \oplus \varepsilon^1$. Here $\varepsilon^1$ is trivial and $L$ is the line bundle over $E$ with $w_1(L) = w_1(E)$.

We use obstruction theory to describe the sections of $S_E$ up to homotopy. Indeed, since the higher homotopy groups of $S^1$ are all trivial, there is a single obstruction to the existence of a section of $S_E$ lying in $H^{2}(E;{\mathbb Z}_w),$ and the obstruction to finding a homotopy of sections lies in $H^{1}(E;{\mathbb Z}_w).$ Thus homotopy classes of sections of $S_E$ are in one-to-one correspondence with elements in $H^{1}(E;{\mathbb Z}_w),$ which is isomorphic to $H_1(E;{\mathbb Z})$ by Poincar\'{e} duality for twisted coefficients.

Let $X = W\times I \smallsetminus\text{int}(N_E)$ and consider the Mayer-Vietoris sequence associated with the decomposition $W\times I = X \cup N_E$:
\begin{equation}\label{mv-seq}
\xymatrix{0 \ar[r]^{} & H_2(S_E;{\mathbb Z}/2)\ar[r]^{\varphi\qquad \quad} & H_2(N_E; {\mathbb Z}/2)\oplus H_2(X; {\mathbb Z}/2)\ar[r]^{\quad \;\; \psi} & H_2(W\times I; {\mathbb Z}/2).}
\end{equation}
Since $[E]=0$ in $H_2(W \times I;{\mathbb Z}/2),$ we have $\psi([E],0) =0$. By exactness, there must exist an element $\alpha \in H_2(S_E;{\mathbb Z}/2)$ with $\varphi(\alpha)=([E],0).$  We will show that $\alpha$ can be represented as the image of a section of $S_E.$

The Gysin sequence for the bundle $p \colon S_E \to E$ gives that
\begin{equation}\label{gysin}
\xymatrix{0 \ar[r]^{} & H^1(E;{\mathbb Z}/2)\ar[r]^{p^{*}} & H^1(S_E; {\mathbb Z}/2)\ar[r]^{f} & H^0(E; {\mathbb Z}/2)\ar[r]^{\smallsmile\, w_2}& H^2(E;{\mathbb Z}/2).}
\end{equation}
Here the second map $f$ is given by evaluating a cohomology class on the circle fiber, and the third map  is trivial since $w_2=w_2(E)=0$. By the sequence \eqref{gysin} and our previous calculations, we have that $H^1(S_E;{\mathbb Z}/2)\cong ({\mathbb Z}/2)^{2k+1}$, thus $H_2(S_E;{\mathbb Z}/2)\cong ({\mathbb Z}/2)^{2k+1}$ by  Poincar\'{e} duality.

Given a section of $S_E$, its image determines an element of $H_2(S_E;{\mathbb Z}/2)$, which we denote $[E']$. We can write $\varphi = (\varphi_1,\varphi_2)$ for the first map of the Mayer-Vietoris sequence \eqref{mv-seq}, and note that $\varphi_1(\alpha) = p_*(\alpha)$ under the natural identification $H_2(N_E;{\mathbb Z}/2) \cong H_2(E;{\mathbb Z}/2)$. For any section, we have $\varphi([E'])=([E],\beta)$ for some $\beta \in H_2(X;{\mathbb Z}/2).$ We claim that the section can be chosen so that $\beta =0,$ namely so that $\varphi([E'])=([E],0)$.

Let $\gamma \in H^1(S_E;{\mathbb Z}/2)$ be the Poincar\'{e} dual of $[E'] \in H_2(S_E;{\mathbb Z}/2).$ According to the Gysin sequence \eqref{gysin}, $f(\gamma) =1$ in $H^0(E;{\mathbb Z}/2)\cong {\mathbb Z}/2$. This holds since the intersection number $[E']\cdot [F] =1$ in $S_E$, where $[F] \in H_1(S_E;{\mathbb Z}/2)$ is the homology class of the circle fiber.

As previously observed, homotopy classes of sections of $S_E$ are in one-to-one correspondence with elements in $H^1(E;{\mathbb Z}_w)$. Let $r \colon H^1(E;{\mathbb Z}_w)\to H^1(E;{\mathbb Z}/2)$ be the map obtained by reducing coefficients mod 2, and note that this map is surjective. The group $H^1(E;{\mathbb Z}_w)$ acts on $H^1(S_E;{\mathbb Z}/2)$ by $\xi \cdot \gamma = \gamma + p^*(r(\xi))$, where $\xi \in H^1(E;{\mathbb Z}_w)$ and $\gamma \in H^1(S_E;{\mathbb Z}/2)$. Note that the action is transitive on the fiber $f^{-1}(1)$ of \eqref{gysin}. Thus every element $\gamma \in H^1(S_E;{\mathbb Z}/2)$ with $f(\gamma)=1$ is the Poincar\'{e} dual of the image $[E']$ of some section of $S_E.$ Correspondingly, every element in $\varphi_1^{-1}([E]) \subset H_2(S_E;{\mathbb Z}/2)$ is the image of some section. In particular, applied  to the element $\alpha \in H_2(S_E;{\mathbb Z}/2)$ with $\varphi(\alpha) =([E],0)$,  this shows that $\alpha$ can be represented by a section. This proves the claim.

Let $[E']$ be the image of a section of $S_E$ with $\varphi([E']) =([E],0)$. Then $E'$ is a compact surface embedded in $S_E$ homeomorphic to $E$. Let $\varphi \colon S_E \to BO$ be the classifying map for the normal bundle of the embedding of $E'$ in $S_E$.

Since $BO={\mathbb R}{\rm P}^\infty = K({\mathbb Z}/2,1)$,  the set of homotopy classes $[S_E,{\mathbb R}{\rm P}^\infty]$ is isomorphic to $H^1(S_E;{\mathbb Z}/2)$. 
Since $S_E$ is compact, the image of $\varphi$ must lie in ${\mathbb R}{\rm P}^N \subset {\mathbb R}{\rm P}^\infty$ for some $N.$  
By the claim, $\varphi$ extends to a map $\varphi \colon X \to {\mathbb R}{\rm P}^N$, 
which we can choose to be transverse to the codimension one submanifold ${\mathbb R}{\rm P}^{N-1} \subset {\mathbb R}{\rm P}^N$. Taking $V' = \varphi^{-1}({\mathbb R}{\rm P}^{N-1})$,  it follows that $V'$ is a compact 3-manifold in $X$ with $\partial V' = E'.$ The manifold $V$ is obtained from $V'$ by attaching a cylinder in $N_E$ which connects $E$ and $E'$.

label: thm-surface-bound
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm-surface-bound}
Let $K\subset \Sigma \times I$ with spanning surface $F \subset \Sigma \times I$. Let $W$ be a handlebody with $\partial W =\Sigma$ and $S \subset W \times I$ an oriented surface with $\partial S =K$. Then there exists a spanning surface $F'$ which is $S^*$-equivalent to $F$ such that $E'=F'\cup S$ bounds a 3-manifold $V\subset W\times I$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By adding half-twisted bands, we can find a spanning surface $F'$ such that $e(F')=0$. Since $S$ is orientable, $e(S)=0$, and it follows that $e(E)=e(F')+e(S)=0$.
 
Since $W$ is a handlebody, we see that $H_2(W\times I; {\mathbb Z}/2)=0$. Thus $[E']=0$. The result now follows from \Cref{boundary}.
head: environment

label: discussion
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{discussion}
Let $K$ be slice, then there is a slice disk $D\subset W\times I$ for some 3-manifold $W$ such that $E=F\cup D$ bounds a 3-manifold $V\subset W\times I$.
head: environment

label: long-exact-seq
title: Proof
body_md:
As before, by adding half-twisted bands, we can arrange that $e(E)=0$.

Consider the long exact sequence in homology for the triple $(W \times I, \Sigma \times I, K)$:
\begin{equation}\label{long-exact-seq}
\xymatrix{H_2(\Sigma \times I, K;{\mathbb Z}/2)\ar[r]^{i_*} & H_2(W \times I, K;{\mathbb Z}/2)\ar[r]^{j_*\quad} &H_2(W \times I, \Sigma \times I;{\mathbb Z}/2).}
\end{equation}


The spanning surface $F$ gives an element $[F] \in H_2(\Sigma \times I, K;{\mathbb Z}/2),$ which maps to $[K] \in H_1(K;{\mathbb Z}/2)$ under the long exact sequence of the pair $(\Sigma \times I, K)$. The homology group $H_2(\Sigma \times I, K;{\mathbb Z}/2)$ is isomorphic to the Klein four-group ${\mathbb Z}/2 \times {\mathbb Z}/2$, and there are exactly two elements in $H_2(\Sigma \times I, K;{\mathbb Z}/2)$ that map to $[K]$. Both occur as the homology class of a spanning surface for $K$.

The slice disk $D$ in $W \times I$ gives an element $[D] \in H_2(W \times I, K;{\mathbb Z}/2)$ which also maps to $[K] \in H_1(K;{\mathbb Z}/2)$ under the long exact sequence of the pair $(W \times I, K)$. Thus, $E=F \cup D$ has $[E]=0$ in $H_2(W \times I;{\mathbb Z}/2)$ provided that $[D]$ pulls back under $i_*$ in \eqref{long-exact-seq} to a class in $H_2(\Sigma \times I, K;{\mathbb Z}/2).$

By exactness of \eqref{long-exact-seq}, we see that $[D]$ pulls back if and only if it lies in the kernel of $j_*$. Thus, the obstruction is the element $j_*([D])$ in 
$$ H_2(W \times I, \Sigma \times I;{\mathbb Z}/2)\cong H_2(W,\Sigma;{\mathbb Z}/2) \cong H^1(W;{\mathbb Z}/2),$$ 
where the first isomorphism follows from $(W \times I, \Sigma \times I) \simeq (W, \Sigma)$ and the second from Poincar\'{e} duality. 
The corresponding element $\gamma \in H^1(W;{\mathbb Z}/2)$ determines a homomorphism $H_1(W;{\mathbb Z}) \to {\mathbb Z}/2$.

Let $\widetilde{W}$ be the associated two-fold cover of W. Then since $\pi_1(\Sigma)$ lies in the kernel of $\gamma$, it restricts to the trivial cover on $\Sigma.$  Therefore, it has two copies of $\Sigma$ in its boundary. Attach a handlebody to one of them to get a 3-manifold with boundary $\Sigma$. Consider now the knot $K$ and spanning surface $F $ in the (thickening of the) boundary of $\widetilde{W}$. 
The disk $D$ lifts to  a slice disk $\widetilde{D}$ in $\widetilde{W} \times I$. 
Notice $[\widetilde{D}]$ maps to zero under the map $H_2(\widetilde{W} \times I, K;{\mathbb Z}/2) \to H_2(\widetilde{W} \times I, \Sigma \times I;{\mathbb Z}/2)$.


The result now follows from \Cref{boundary}.
head: environment

label: kernel
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{kernel}
There is a generating set $\{\gamma_1, \ldots, \gamma_{2g}\}$ for $H_1(F; {\mathbb Z})$ such that $\gamma_1, \ldots, \gamma_{g}$ lie in the kernel of the map $H_1(F;{\mathbb Z}) \to H_1(V;{\mathbb Q}).$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $i\colon E\to V$ be the inclusion map. First assume $V$ is orientable. Then by \cite[VI, Theorem 10.4]{Bredon} and/or \cite[Lemma  3.5]{Hatcher-2007}, $\,{\rm dim}\,(\,{\rm Ker}\,i_{*})=\frac{1}{2} \,{\rm dim}\,(H_1(E;{\mathbb Q}))$. By a Mayer-Vietoris argument, $H_1(F; {\mathbb Z})\cong H_1(E; {\mathbb Z})$, and by the Universal Coefficient Theorem, $H_1(E; {\mathbb Z})\otimes {\mathbb Q}\cong H_1(E; {\mathbb Q})$, and the conclusion follows in this case.

Now assume $V$ is not orientable.
If $i_{*}\colon H_1(E;{\mathbb Z}/2)\to H_1(V;{\mathbb Z}/2)$, then $\,{\rm dim}\,(\,{\rm Ker}\,i_{*}) =\frac{1}{2} \,{\rm dim}\,(H_1(E;{\mathbb Z}/2))$. We can choose a generating set $\{\gamma_1, \ldots, \gamma_{2g}\}$ for $H_1(F; {\mathbb Z})$, such that the mod 2 reduction of $\{\gamma_1, \ldots, \gamma_{g}\}$ generates $\,{\rm Ker}\,i_{*}$, so they must all be mapped to torsion elements in $H_1(V;{\mathbb Z})$, and therefore, they all lie in the kernel of the map $H_1(F;{\mathbb Z}) \to H_1(V;{\mathbb Q}).$
head: environment

label: slice
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{slice}
Let $K \subset \Sigma \times I$ be a knot with spanning surface $F$ such that $e(F)=0$. Suppose further that $K$ is slice. Then
$$|\sigma(K,F)|\leq n(K,F).$$ 
In particular, if $n(K,F)=0$, then $\sigma(K,F)=0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \Cref{discussion} there is a slice disk $D\subset W\times I$ for some 3-manifold $W$ such that $E=F\cup D$ bounds a 3-manifold $V\subset W\times I$.
Now by \Cref{kernel}, we have a set $\{ \gamma_1, \ldots, \gamma_{2g}\}$ of generators for $H_1(F;{\mathbb Z})$ such that $\gamma_1, \ldots, \gamma_{g}$ lie in the kernel of the map $H_1(F;{\mathbb Z}) \to H_1(V;{\mathbb Q}).$ Let $U$ be the subgroup of $H_1(F;{\mathbb Z})$ generated by $\gamma_1, \ldots, \gamma_{g}$. For any $a\in U$, there is a surface $A$ with boundary a multiple of $a$. Now suppose $b\in U$, and $B$ is a surface with boundary a multiple of $b$. We have
$$\mathcal G_{F}(a,b)=\tfrac{1}{2}(\operatorname{\ell{\it k}}(\tau a,b)+\operatorname{\ell{\it k}}(\tau b,a)).$$
Let $N(V)$ be a tubular neighborhood of $V$ in $W \times I$. Then $N(V)$ is a (possibly twisted) $I$-bundle over $V$ with boundary $\partial N(V)$ a $\{\pm 1\}$-bundle over $V$. If $p\colon N(V) \to V$ is the projection map, then $p^{-1}(A) \cap \partial N(V)$ gives a surface $\widetilde{A}$ in $W \times I$ with boundary $\tau a$. (In fact, $p|_{\widetilde{A}}\colon  \widetilde{A} \to A$ is a two-fold covering.) Notice that $\widetilde{A}$ and $B$ are disjoint, hence the intersection $\widetilde{A} \cdot B =0.$ Thus,  $\operatorname{\ell{\it k}}(\tau a,b) = \widetilde{A} \cdot B = 0$. A similar argument shows that $\operatorname{\ell{\it k}}(\tau b,a)=0$. Thus $\mathcal G_{F}(a,b)=0$ for $a,b \in U.$ Hence $U$ is a totally isotropic subspace for the Gordon-Litherland pairing. Equation \eqref{max_total_isot} gives the inequality:
$$2\dim U \leq \dim H_1(F;{\mathbb Z})-|\operatorname{sig} (\mathcal G_{F})|+n(K,F),$$ but since $\dim U = \tfrac{1}{2} \dim H_1(F;{\mathbb Z})$ in our case, it follows that  $|\operatorname{sig} (\mathcal G_{F})|\leq n(K,F).$

Now the self-intersection number of $E$, which is the normal Euler number of $E$, vanishes. To calculate
the self-intersection number of $E$, we push a copy of $E$ off itself.
Since the slice disk $D$ is orientable, we can push it off so there are no self-intersection points over the slice disk. Therefore, the intersection number is
$-\operatorname{\ell{\it k}}(K,K')=e(F,K)=0$. It follows that $|\operatorname{sig}\mathcal G_F|=|\sigma(K,F)|\leq n(K,F).$

title: Remark
body_md:
For a null-homologous knot $K \subset \Sigma 	imes I$ with Seifert surface $F\subset \Sigma 	imes I$, 
one can show that $\det(K,F)= 
abla^{+}_{K,F}(-1)=
abla^{-}_{K,F}(-1)$. Here $
abla^{\pm}_{K,F}(t)$ refers to the directed Alexander polynomial defined in \S 2.4 of \cite{Boden-Chrisman-Gaudreau-2020}. Thus, for these knots, \Cref{determinant} can be deduced from Theorem 2.8 of\cite{Boden-Chrisman-Gaudreau-2020}, giving the Fox-Milnor condition that $
abla^{\pm}_{K,F}(t) = f^{\pm}(t)f^{\pm}(t^{-1})$ for some $f^\pm(t) \in {\mathbb Z}[t]$ when $K$ is slice.

label: thm-sign
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $k= g(S)$. Since $E=F \cup S$ bounds a 3-manifold, it follows that $H_1(F; {\mathbb Z})$ has even rank, say $2h$. Furthermore, since $S$ is orientable, $F$ has normal Euler number $e(F)=e(E)=0.$
In the case $k \geq h$, then the conclusion follows trivially from the fact that $|\sigma(K,F)|=|\operatorname{sig} \mathcal G_F|\leq 2h.$ Therefore, we can assume that $k<h.$

We can repeat the proof of \Cref{kernel}, to show that there is a generating set $\{\gamma_1, \ldots, \gamma_{2h}\}$ for $H_1(F; {\mathbb Z})$
such that $\gamma_1, \ldots, \gamma_{h-k}$ lie in the kernel of the map $H_1(F;{\mathbb Z}) \to H_1(V;{\mathbb Q}).$

For a symmetric bilinear form with rank $r$, signature $\sigma$, and nullity $n$, by \Cref{max_total_isot}, any totally isotropic subspace has rank at most  $(r-|\sigma|+n)/2$. Hence
$$h-k\leq (2h-|\operatorname{sig} \mathcal G_{F}|+n(K,F))/2,$$
and the conclusion follows.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
\Cref{thm-sign} is easiest to apply in case $W$ is a handlebody. 

Let $K \subset \Sigma \times I$ be a knot with spanning surface $F$, and $S \subset  W\times I$ is an orientable surface of genus $g$. If $W$ is a handlebody, then by \Cref{thm-surface-bound}, there is a spanning surface $F'$ that is $S^*$-equivalent to $F$ such that $E' = F' \cup S$  bounds a 3-manifold $V$. In particular, since $F$ and $F'$ are $S^*$-equivalent, $\sigma(K,F) =\sigma(K,F)$ and $n(K,F) =n(K,F')$. Applying \Cref{thm-sign} to $F'$, it follows that 
$$|\sigma(K,F)| \leq 2g(S) + n(K,F).$$

label: defn:123
title: Definition
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: Let $K \subset \Sigma \times I$ be a knot in a thickened surface represented by a cellularly embedded, alternating diagram. Let $F$ and $F^*$ be the two checkerboard surfaces associated to the coloring. Then $\det(K,F)\neq 0$ and $\det(K,F^*)\neq 0$. Further, $|\sigma(K,F)-\sigma(K,F^*)| =2g,$ where $g$ is the genus of $\Sigma.$ In particular, if $\Sigma$ has genus $g\geq 1,$ then $K$ is not slice.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Using Lemma 6 
of \cite{Boden-Karimi-2020}, we see that $K$ admits a positive definite and negative definite spanning surface. Since there are only two $S^*$-equivalence classes of surfaces, it follows that one of the definite spanning surfaces is $S^*$-equivalent to $F$ and the other is $S^*$-equivalent to $F^*$. In particular, since $\det(K,F)$ depends only on the $S^*$-equivalence class of $F$, it follows that $\det(K,F)\neq 0$ and $\det(K,F^*)\neq 0$.

Arguing as in the proof of Theorem 19 
of \cite{Boden-Karimi-2020}, we see that $|\sigma(K,F)-\sigma(K,F^*)| =2g$. We then apply \Cref{cor-slice} to conclude that $K$ is not slice.

label: unimodular
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{unimodular}
If $M,M'$ are two symmetric integral $n\times n$ matrices that are unimodular congruent, then ${\upbeta}(\varphi_{M})={\upbeta}(\varphi_{M'}).$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix a basis $\{e_1,\ldots, e_n\}$ for $U$. For an element $u\in U$, by abuse of notation, denote the coordinate of $u$ with respect to the basis (an $n\times 1$ column) also by $u$.

Let $B,B'$ be the symmetric bilinear forms on $U$ determined by $M,M',$ respectively. 
Since they are unimodular congruent, we have $M'=P^{\mathsf{T}}MP$ for some unimodular matrix $P$. 
                                                
Then
$$B'(u,v)=u^{\mathsf{T}}M' v=u^{\mathsf{T}}P^{\mathsf{T}}M P v=B( Pu,Pv).$$
It follows that
$$\varphi_{M'}([u])= \varphi_{M}([Pu])=\varphi_{M}(\Phi[u]), $$
where $\Phi\colon V\to V$ is given by $\Phi([u])=[Pu]$. Since $P$ is unimodular, $\Phi$ is an isomorphism. Thus $\varphi_{M'}=\varphi_{M} \circ \Phi$, and by \cite[Definition 1.19]{Brown}, we see that $\varphi_{M}$ and $\varphi_{M'}$ are isomorphic. The result now follows from \cite[Theorem 1.20, (i)]{Brown}.

label: ex-3-5-1
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex-3-5-1}
\Cref{fig-3-5-1} shows a knot in the thickened torus with two spanning surfaces $F$ (middle) and $F^*$ (right). 

For the first surface, using the basis $\{x_1,x_2\}$ for $H_1(F;{\mathbb Z})$, we compute that the Gordon-Litherland pairing $\mathcal G_F$ is given by the diagonal matrix $[1]\oplus [-2]$.
Thus, we can represent $\varphi_F$ by the special matrix $[1]\oplus [2]$.
As previously noted, the form represented by $[2]$ is not proper, nor is any form containing $[2]$ as an orthogonal summand. 
Therefore,  ${\upbeta}(\varphi_F)=\infty,$ and ${\upbeta}_{F}(K)=\infty$ is undefined. 

For the second surface, using the basis $\{x_1,x_2,x_3\}$ for $H_1(F^*;{\mathbb Z})$, we compute the Gordon-Litherland pairing $\mathcal G_{F^*}$ and see that 
$\varphi_{F^*}$ is represented by the special matrix 
$$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\  * & 0 & 1 \\ * & * & 0\end{bmatrix}.$$ 
A straightforward calculation reveals that 
$\lambda(\varphi_{F^*})= 2+2i =(\sqrt{2})^3e^{ {\pi i} /4}. $
Therefore, ${\upbeta}(\varphi_{F^*})=1$. Since $e(F^{*},K)=2$, it follows that ${\upbeta}_{F^*}(K)= 1+\frac{1}{2}e(F^{*},K)=2$.
\hfill $\Diamond$

label: GL-pairing
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{GL-pairing}
The Goeritz matrix $G_\xi(D)$ is the $n \times n$ matrix obtained by deleting the first row and column from $G'_{\xi}(D).$ In other words, $G_\xi(D) =(g_{ij})_{i,j=1,\ldots, n}.$

body_md:
\label{ex-3-5-2}
\Cref{fig-3-5} shows the same knot as in the \Cref{ex-3-5-1}, along with the Tait graphs for $F$ (middle) and for $F^*$ (right). 

For the surface $F$, the associated Goeritz matrix is empty. Hence, ${\upbeta}(\varphi_{\xi})=0$. We have $\mu_{\xi}=-2$, and ${\upbeta}_{\xi}(K)=0-(-2)=2$.

For the surface $F^*$, the associated Goeritz matrix is $G_{\xi^*}(D)=[2]$, which we have seen represents an improper form. Thus, ${\upbeta}(\varphi_{\xi^*})=\infty$, and so ${\upbeta}_{\xi^*}(K)=\infty$ is undefined.

label: thm:chrom-dual
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:chrom-dual}
Let $F \subset \Sigma \times I$ be a connected spanning surface such that the map $H_1(F;{\mathbb Z}/2) \to H_1(\Sigma \times I;{\mathbb Z}/2)$ is surjective. Let $F'=F\#_\tau \Sigma$ be as above, and set  $\mathcal K_F= \operatorname{Ker} (H_1(F;{\mathbb Z}/2) \to H_1(\Sigma \times I;{\mathbb Z}/2))$. Then the Brown invariant of $\varphi_{F'}$ is equal to the Brown invariant of the restriction of $\varphi_F$ to $\mathcal K_F,$ i.e., ${\upbeta}(\varphi_{F'}) = {\upbeta}(\varphi|_{\mathcal K_F})$.
head: environment

label: eqn:big-matrix
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $g =g(\Sigma)$ be the  genus of $\Sigma$. As in the proof of \cite[Theorem 4.1]{Boden-Chrisman-Karimi-2021}, we can choose a basis for $H_1(F';{\mathbb Z})$ such that the Gordon-Litherland matrix has block decomposition 
\begin{equation} \label{eqn:big-matrix}
M=\begin{bmatrix} A&*& 0 \\ *&B & J_g \\ 0&J_g^\mathsf{T} & 0 \end{bmatrix},
\end{equation}
where $A$ is the $n \times n$ matrix for the restriction of $\mathcal G_{F}$ to $\operatorname{Ker} (H_1(F;{\mathbb Z}) \to H_1(\Sigma \times I;{\mathbb Z}))$, and 
$$J_g=\begin{bmatrix} 0& I_g \\ -I_g & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ 
is the standard $2g \times 2g$ symplectic matrix representing the intersection form on $\Sigma$. (Here $I_g$ denotes the $g \times g$ identity matrix.)

The matrix in \eqref{eqn:big-matrix} is unimodular congruent to one of the form:
\begin{equation*}\label{eqn:big-matrix-2}
M'=\begin{bmatrix} A&0& 0 \\ 0&B & J_g \\ 0&J_g^\mathsf{T} & 0 \end{bmatrix}.
\end{equation*}
Therefore, by \Cref{unimodular}, it follows that ${\upbeta}(\varphi_{F'}) = {\upbeta}(\varphi_{M})={\upbeta}(\varphi_{M'})$. 

A non-singular ${\mathbb Z}/4$ quadratic form $\phi \colon V \to {\mathbb Z}/4$ is said to be \textit{metabolic} if there exists a half-dimensional subspace $H \subset V$ such that $\phi$ vanishes on $H$. (In \cite[\S 4]{Matsumoto}, this is defined as \textit{split}.) By \cite[Lemma 4.1]{Matsumoto}, if $\phi$ is metabolic, then
${\upbeta}(\phi)=0$. Since the Brown invariant is additive under orthogonal sum,
and since the quadratic form associated to 
$$\begin{bmatrix} B & J_g \\ J_g^\mathsf{T} & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ is clearly metabolic,
                                     
it follows that ${\upbeta}(\varphi_{M'})={\upbeta}(\varphi_A).$ However, $\varphi_A$ is equal to the restricted ${\mathbb Z}/4$ quadratic form $\varphi|_{\mathcal K_F},$ and the result now follows.
head: environment

label: thm:chromatic
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:chromatic}
Let $D \subset \Sigma$ be a cellularly embedded, checkerboard colorable link diagram with coloring $\xi$,
and let $F$ be its black checkerboard surface. Let $\xi^*$ be the opposite coloring and $F^*$ its black checkerboard surface. (Thus $F^*$ is the white surface for $\xi.$)
The two sets of Brown invariants are related by chromatic duality:
${\upbeta}_{F}(D) = {\upbeta}_{\xi^*}(D)$ and ${\upbeta}_{F^*}(D) = {\upbeta}_{\xi}(D)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The proof follows from \Cref{thm:chrom-dual} and \cite[Lemma 5.3]{Boden-Chrisman-Karimi-2021}.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: At first glance, it may seem that the switch of colorings in \Cref{thm:chromatic} is the result of an incompatibility in the choice of conventions. However, it is unavoidable, and in fact it is an intrinsic aspect, and a curious one at that. This aspect is not readily apparent for classical links since the two sets of invariants are always equal in that case.
head: environment

label: cobordism
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{cobordism}
Let $K \subset \Sigma\times I$ be a knot with spanning surface $F\subset \Sigma\times I$. Assume $e(F,K)=0$ and $\det(\mathcal G_F) \not\equiv 0 \text{ (mod $2$)}$. If $K$ is slice, then ${\upbeta}_{F}(K)=0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $K$ is slice, then \Cref{slice} implies that the Gordon-Litherland pairing is metabolic,
namely that $\mathcal G_F$ vanishes on a half-dimensional subspace $U$ of $H_1(F;{\mathbb Z})$. It follows that $\varphi_F$ must vanish on the image of $U$ under the mod 2 projection
$H_1(F;{\mathbb Z}) \to H_1(F;{\mathbb Z}/2)$. The image is
again a half-dimensional subspace of
$H_1(F;{\mathbb Z}/2)$. 


Theorem 1.20 (ix) in \cite{Brown} implies that the Brown invariant vanishes on any non-singular, metabolic quadratic space (see also \cite[Lemma 4.1]{Matsumoto}). Therefore, ${\upbeta}(\varphi_F)=0$. Since $e(F,K)=0$, it follows that ${\upbeta}_{F}(K)=0$.
head: environment

label: prop:mirror_image
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cite[Proposition 5.7]{Boden-Chrisman-Karimi-2021}, $\mathcal G_{L^*,F^*} = - \mathcal G_{L,F},$ and $e(F^*,L^*) = -e(F,L).$ The result now follows from \Cref{defn:Brown-link} and \cite[Theorem 1.20, (iii)]{Brown}. A similar argument shows that
$\mathcal G_{L^\dag,F^\dag} = - \mathcal G_{L,F},$ and $e(F^\dag,L^\dag) = -e(F,L),$ and the
 formula for ${\upbeta}_{F^\dag}(L^\dag)$ follows.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
If $K\subset \Sigma \times I$ is a null-homologous knot with Seifert surface $F$,
and $\det(K,F)\not\equiv 0 \text{ (mod $2$)}$, then 
$${\upbeta}_{F}(K)=4\operatorname{Arf}(q_{K,F}).$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By the definitions of $q_{K,F}$ and $\varphi_{F}$, we see that $\varphi_{F}=2q_{K,F}$. The result then follows from \cite[Theorem 1.20, (vii)]{Brown}.
head: environment

label: ex-6-87310
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex-6-87310}
\Cref{fig-6-87310} shows a six crossing knot $K$ in the thickened torus, along with the Tait graphs for the checkerboard surfaces $F$ (middle) and $F^*$ (right). 

For the surface $F$, the associated Goeritz matrix is 
$$G_{\xi}(D)=\left[
\begin{matrix}
1&-1&-1\\
*&1&-1\\
*&*&1
\end{matrix}
\right].$$ 
We have $\lambda(\varphi_{\xi})=4+4i$. Notice that $\varphi_\xi$ is singular and proper with ${\upbeta}(\varphi_{\xi})=1$. We have $\mu_{\xi}=-3$, therefore ${\upbeta}_{\xi}(K)=1-(-3)=4$.

For the surface $F^*$, the associated Goeritz matrix is 
$G_{\xi^*}(D)=[-3]$. Then $\lambda(\varphi_{\xi^*})=1+i$ and  ${\upbeta}(\varphi_{\xi^*})=1$. Further $\mu_{\xi^*}=-3$, thus ${\upbeta}_{\xi^*}(K)=1-(-3)=4$.

Notice that $K$ is null-homologous, in fact it is the knot $6.87310$ in Figure 21 of  \cite{Boden-Chrisman-Gaudreau-2020}. Let $F'$ be the Seifert surface whose Seifert matrices are listed in \cite[Table 3]{Boden-Chrisman-Gaudreau-2020}.
Then $F'$ is $S^*$-equivalent to $F$, and its quadratic form $q_{K,F'}$ is singular and proper. Since ${\upbeta}_{\xi}(K)=4$, it follows that $\operatorname{Arf}(q_{K,F'})=1.$
\hfill $\Diamond$

label: concordance
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Define $\Theta$ on $H_1(F_0;{\mathbb Z})\oplus H_1(F_1;{\mathbb Z})$ as follows
$$\Theta((x_0,x_1),(y_0,y_1))=-\mathcal G_{F_0}(x_0,y_0)+\mathcal G_{F_1}(x_1,y_1).$$
By \Cref{kernel-2}, and similar to the proof of \Cref{slice}, $\gamma_1, \ldots, \gamma_{m_0},\gamma'_1,\ldots,\gamma'_{m_1}$
generate a totally isotropic subspace for $\Theta$. Since the nullity of $\Theta$ is zero, it follows that
$$2(m_0+m_1)=g_0+g_1\leq g_0+g_1-|\operatorname{sig} \Theta|,$$
so $0=\operatorname{sig}\Theta=-\operatorname{sig}\mathcal G_{F_0}+\operatorname{sig}\mathcal G_{F_1}$, which implies $\operatorname{sig}\mathcal G_{F_0}=\operatorname{sig}\mathcal G_{F_1}$.

Again, the self-intersection number of $E$ vanishes. The self-intersection number of $E$ equals
$$-\operatorname{\ell{\it k}}(K_0,K_{0}')+\operatorname{\ell{\it k}}(K_1,K_{1}')=-e(F_0,K_0)+e(F_1,K_1)=0.$$
It follows that $e(F_0,K_0)=e(F_1,K_1)$, and $\sigma(K_0,F_0)=\sigma(K_1,F_1).$
head: environment

label: brown-concordance
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the mod 2 reduction of the form $\Theta$ defined in the proof of \Cref{concordance}. Now define $\Phi:H_1(F_0;{\mathbb Z}/2)\oplus H_1(F_1;{\mathbb Z}/2) \to {\mathbb Z}/4$, as $\Phi([a],[b])\equiv -\mathcal G_{F_0}(a,a)+\mathcal G_{F_1}(b,b)\text{ (mod $4$)}$. We can check that $\Phi$ is a quadratic enhancement, and we can define ${\upbeta}(\Phi)$.
  
Similar to \Cref{cobordism}, we deduce that ${\upbeta}(\Phi)=0$. Notice that the Brown invariant is additive, and that ${\upbeta}(-\varphi)\equiv -{\upbeta}(\varphi) \text{ (mod $8$)}$. The result now follows.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $K_0\subset \Sigma_0\times I$ and $K_1\subset \Sigma_1\times I$ be knots with spanning surfaces $F_0 \subset \Sigma_0 \times I$ and $F_1 \subset \Sigma_1 \times I$, respectively.
If $K_0$ and $K_1$ are concordant, then there exists an oriented 3-manifold $W$ with $\partial W =\Sigma_1 \sqcup -\Sigma_0$ and a properly embedded annulus $A$ in $W \times I$ with $\partial A = K_0 \sqcup K_1$. Let $E=F_0\cup A\cup F_1$. If 
$[E]=0$ in $H_2(W\times I; {\mathbb Z}/2)$, then $F_0$ and $F_1$ are concordant.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We can arrange that $e(F_0,K_0)=e(F_1,K_1)$, so $e(E)=0$. Since $[E]=0,$ then \Cref{boundary} implies that there exists a compact 3-manifold $V\subset W\times I$ with $\partial V=E$.
The result now follows.
